text: A "living [[fossil|fossil]]" is a plant or animal alive today that looks very much like relatives known only from very old [[@fossils-form|fossils]]. Its family has been around for tens or hundreds of millions of years without changing its basic body plan very much.

Famous examples include the coelacanth, a deep-sea fish, the horseshoe crab, the ginkgo tree and the nautilus, a shelled cousin of the octopus. Charles Darwin first used the phrase in 1859. Many scientists today use it with care, because these creatures have kept [[evolution|evolving]]. They have just changed slowly on the outside.

st.prompt: Before 1938, how long did scientists think coelacanths had been extinct?

options.t: About 66 million years, since the time of the dinosaurs
About 500 years
About 10,000 years, since the last ice age

st.reveal: Coelacanth fossils stop appearing in rocks around the time the dinosaurs died out, so experts assumed the fish had vanished then too. The living fish had simply been hiding in deep water off Africa, where nobody had looked.

n.certNote: Many biologists dislike the term "living fossil", because these species have kept evolving. They prefer phrases like "slowly changing lineage", and they argue about which animals and plants should count.

myth: Living fossils have not changed at all for millions of years.

They have kept evolving, like every living thing. Their overall body shape has stayed similar, but their genes and many details have changed. Today's coelacanths, for example, are different species from the ones found as fossils.

sec.t:
Horseshoe [[@crabs|crabs]] are not true crabs. They are more closely related to spiders and scorpions. Fossils of their relatives go back about 450 million years, long before the first dinosaurs. Each year, they still crawl onto beaches in the USA and Asia to lay eggs, including in Odisha and West Bengal. Their blue blood is even used in medicine, to test whether [[vaccine|vaccines]] and injections are free of harmful germs.

The ginkgo tree has fan-shaped leaves that look almost exactly like fossil leaves more than 200 million years old. Wild ginkgos nearly vanished, but monks in China planted them in temple gardens for centuries. Now they line streets in New York, Tokyo and many other cities.

In 2003, the Indian scientist S. D. Biju and his Belgian colleague Franky Bossuyt described a strange frog from the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]]. It is purple-grey, plump and has a small pointed snout, a bit like a balloon with a nose. It spends most of the year underground, eating termites, and comes up only for a few days during the [[monsoon|monsoon]] to breed.

Its closest living relatives are tiny frogs on the Seychelles islands. That fits a much bigger story. Over 100 million years ago, India, the Seychelles and Madagascar were joined together. As [[@india-drift|India drifted]] north, the frog's ancestors were carried with it, and the two families went their separate ways.

There is no single reason. Many living fossils live in places that have stayed fairly steady for a very long time, such as the deep sea or quiet forest floors. Their body plan already works well there, so there is little pressure to change shape.

Some are also tough generalists. Like [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]], horseshoe crabs can eat many foods and survive long periods with little to eat. That may have helped them get through mass [[@extinction|extinctions]] that wiped out more specialised animals.

Some [[biologist|biologists]] say "living fossil" is misleading, because it suggests evolution has stopped. When scientists studied coelacanth [[gene|genes]], they found they had changed more slowly than in many fish, but they had certainly changed.

Others think the phrase is useful, as long as people understand it loosely. Whatever you call them, these animals and plants act like windows into the deep past. Looking at a living horseshoe crab gives scientists clues about how its ancient relatives may have moved, fed and laid eggs.

text: Triceratops means "three-horned face". It had two long horns above its eyes, a short one on its nose, and a wide bony frill at the back of its head. It was a plant-eater as long as a school bus and heavier than an elephant.

Its horns and frill probably did several jobs. Healed wounds show that Triceratops fought each other, locking horns like deer. The horns could also have been used against hungry [[@trex-bite|T. rex]]. The frill was big, bold and easy to see, so it may have helped Triceratops recognise each other and show off.

st.prompt: Scientists checked many Triceratops skulls for healed injuries. Where did they find the most?

options.t: On the frill and cheeks, where another Triceratops's horns would hit
On the tail, where a T. rex would bite
Nowhere, because the frill was too hard to hurt

st.reveal: The healed wounds were mostly on the sides of the frill and face. That is exactly where the horns of a rival would land if two Triceratops locked heads and pushed, as deer and antelope do today.

src: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of Natural History, Triceratops.
Farke A.A., Wolff E.D.S. and Tanke D.H. (2009) Evidence of combat in Triceratops. PLoS ONE 4.
n.certNote: Healed wounds show that Triceratops really did fight. How much the horns and frill were for fighting, defence or showing off is still argued about.

myth: Scientists decided Triceratops never existed and renamed it.
That story spread online in 2010 and it is wrong. Some scientists suggested that Torosaurus might be a grown-up Triceratops. If so, the older name, Triceratops, would be kept.

sec.t:
In 1887, a pair of large horn cores was found near Denver, in the USA. The famous [[fossil|fossil]] hunter Othniel Marsh thought they came from an enormous ancient bison and named it as one. Two years later, more complete skulls turned up in Wyoming. Marsh realised his mistake and named the animal Triceratops in 1889.

Since then, hundreds of Triceratops fossils have been dug up, many in Montana and the Dakotas. It is one of the most common big dinosaurs from the end of the dinosaur age. It shared those floodplains with [[@trex-montana|T. rex]].

Triceratops did meet T. rex. Some Triceratops bones carry T. rex tooth marks. One Triceratops skull has a brow horn that was bitten off and then healed, which means the Triceratops survived the attack. That is good evidence that some Triceratops stood their ground and lived.

Still, horns that were useful against a rival would also help against a [[predator|predator]]. One use does not rule out the other. Rhinos today use their horns both ways, and a rhino's horn is made of [[keratin|keratin]], the same material as your hair.

sec.h: A frill that changed with age
sec.t:
Baby Triceratops had short horns that curved backwards and a small frill with a wavy edge. As they grew, the horns turned to point forwards and the frill became broader. Grown-ups looked quite different from youngsters, a bit like the way a stag grows [[antler|antlers]] that a fawn does not have.

The frill itself was solid bone, which is unusual. Many of its relatives had frills with two large holes in them, covered only by skin. A frill full of holes would make a poor shield, so in those animals display seems the likelier job. The surface of the bone is covered in grooves where blood vessels ran, and some scientists once suggested the frill helped shed heat. Few think that was its main job now.

The way heads changed with age is one more reason scientists think the horns and frill were signals. An adult could tell at a glance who was young, who was grown and who was a rival. Like a [[@peacock-tail|peacock's tail]], a showy head may have mattered as much as a sharp one.

Triceratops is now the state fossil of South Dakota and the state dinosaur of Wyoming. Not bad for an animal once mistaken for a cow's cousin.

text: Rainbow mountains are made of layers of rock, each a different colour. Over millions of years, mud, sand and volcanic ash settled in lakes, rivers and plains, one layer on top of another. Different minerals and different [[climate|climates]] gave each layer its own colour. Later, the rock was pressed into stone, squeezed and pushed up, so the stripes are now tilted and folded into hills.

The colours mostly come from tiny amounts of metals in the rock, especially iron. When iron meets oxygen, it turns red, like [[@rust|rust]]. Where there was little oxygen, the same iron can look green or grey. Wind and rain then wear away the surface, revealing the stripes.

st.prompt: In the Painted Hills of Oregon, USA, what were the coloured layers made from long ago?

options.t: Volcanic ash that slowly turned into clay
Paint spilled by early settlers
Coloured sand blown from the ocean

st.reveal: Ash from volcanoes fell over millions of years and turned into claystone. The climate kept changing, so each layer weathered differently. Wet, warm times left red layers, and drier times left yellow and tan ones.

src: UNESCO Global Geoparks, Zhangye UNESCO Global Geopark.

d.try: In a tall clear jar, pour layers of different coloured things from the kitchen, such as salt, turmeric-mixed salt, rice, red lentils and tea leaves. Tilt the jar gently and watch the layers bend. Rainbow mountains are layers like these, laid flat and then tilted by moving rock.
myth: Rainbow mountain photos look just like the real thing.
Many online photos have their colours turned up. In real life, the stripes are usually softer, rusty reds, ochres and greens. They are still striking, especially after rain or at sunrise.
facts: often iron in low-oxygen minerals, or chlorite

sec.h: Pages in a book of rock
sec.t:
Each layer of [[sediment|sediment]] is a bit like a page in a diary. It records what the land was like at the time. A red layer may mean a hot, dry period when iron rusted in the air. A grey or green layer may mean the mud lay under still water, where oxygen was scarce. A pale layer might be sandstone from an old desert.

[[geologist|Geologists]] read these stripes from the bottom up, oldest first. The [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] in the USA has similar layers, but they are mostly flat. Rainbow mountains are special because their layers have been tilted, so many colours show side by side.

Vinicunca, in the Andes of [[@peru|Peru]], rises to about 5,200 metres, higher than any peak in the Alps. Its stripes are red, purple, yellow and green. For many years, much of it was hidden under snow. Local guides say that as the snow cover shrank, the colours became easier to see, and in the mid-2010s photos spread online.

Now thousands of visitors may climb up on a busy day, many on horseback. The air is thin, so it is a hard walk. The sudden fame has brought money to local villages, but also worries about [[erosion|erosion]] and crowds.

In Oregon, USA, the Painted Hills are low, rounded mounds striped red, gold and black. About 35 million years ago, volcanoes spread ash across the region. The ash turned into soft clay. As the climate changed between warm and wet and cooler and drier, each layer weathered into a different colour.

The black streaks are partly from old plant matter. The hills change colour with the weather too. After rain, the clay soaks up water and looks darker and brighter.

Each mineral gives its own colour. Iron oxide makes reds and oranges. A green mineral called chlorite, and iron without much oxygen, make greens. Some yellow minerals contain iron too, in a different form. Carbon from old plants and animals makes black.

It is a bit like a painter's palette, laid down by nature over millions of years. And the strangest part? Just a handful of minerals make all those shades, much as an artist can [[@colour-mix|mix many colours]] from only a few tubes of paint.

text: If all the trees disappeared, the air wouldn't run out of oxygen any time soon. The [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] holds a huge store of it, and tiny [[plankton|plankton]] in the oceans make about half of each year's new supply. But almost everything else would change.

Huge amounts of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], the gas that traps heat, would no longer be soaked up, so the planet would warm faster. Rain would change, because forests pump water into the air. Soil on hillsides would wash away. Millions of kinds of animals, [[fungus|fungi]] and plants that live in forests would lose their homes. And people would lose wood, paper, rubber, many fruits, spices and medicines.

Within a few days

st.reveal: The air holds an enormous store of oxygen, built up over millions of years, and ocean plankton make about half of the new oxygen each year. Losing trees would cause many disasters, but suffocating wouldn't be the first.

myth: Trees make most of the oxygen we breathe.

Land plants, including trees, make about half of the world's new oxygen. Tiny plankton in the ocean make the other half. Forests also use up much of their own oxygen at night and as they rot, so they matter more for climate, water and wildlife than for our next breath.

sec.t:
In 2015, scientists combined satellite images with counts made on the ground and estimated that Earth has about three trillion trees, roughly 400 for every person. They also estimated that people cut down about 15 billion trees each year, and that there are only about half as many trees now as when people first began farming.

Trees are giant carbon stores. Through [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], they pull carbon dioxide from the air and lock the carbon into wood. Burn or rot that wood, and the carbon goes back into the sky. That's a big part of the [[@carbon-cycle|carbon cycle]], and why losing forests speeds up [[climate|climate]] change.

Tree roots hold soil together like the threads of a net. When hillsides are cleared, heavy rain can wash the soil away, choking rivers with mud and causing landslides. Lost topsoil can take hundreds of years to form again.

On remote [[@easter-island|Easter Island]] in the Pacific, forests of giant palm trees once grew. By about the 1600s, nearly all were gone. People cleared land for farms, and rats that arrived with them ate the palm seeds. Historians still argue about how much this harmed the islanders, but the trees never came back on their own.

Trees work like air conditioners. Their shade blocks sunlight, and water evaporating from leaves cools the air. A tree-lined street can be several degrees cooler than a bare one on a hot afternoon. A city with no trees would bake.

Forests are also home to most of the land's animals and plants. Without trees, tigers, orangutans, hornbills, many monkeys and countless insects would vanish, along with mushrooms and lichens that grow only on wood. Even the [[@banyan|banyan]], home to hundreds of creatures in a single tree, would be gone.

Strangely, Earth has been treeless before. For billions of years, the land was bare rock, mats of [[microbe|microbes]] and, later, small plants. The first true forests appeared about 385 million years ago. Their buried remains later turned into some of the coal people dig up today.

People have fought hard for trees. In the 1970s, women in the Himalayan foothills hugged trees to stop loggers, in what became the [[@chipko|Chipko]] movement. And the strangest part? Many trees can't make fruit or seeds without tiny partners, so forests could also fall apart in a [[@what-if-no-insects|world without insects]].

text: Mars is so far away that a radio message takes between about 3 and 22 minutes to get there. It depends on where the two planets are in their [[@spacecraft-move|orbits]]. So nobody can steer a [[rover|rover]] live, the way you would steer a remote-control car.

Instead, every day scientists send the rover a list of goals: drive to that rock, take pictures, drill here. The rover uses its cameras and computer to map the ground in front of it, spot rocks and slopes, and choose a safe path by itself. Then it reports back with pictures, and the team plans the next day.

Messages take minutes to travel each way
The rover has no wheels

st.reveal: Radio signals take between about 3 and 22 minutes to cross the gap. By the time the rover heard 'stop!', it might already have driven off a cliff. So it plans much of its own route.

d.try: Play rover. One person is the rover and keeps their eyes closed. The "mission control" team must write down every command first ("3 steps forward, turn right"), then read the whole list out at once and stay silent while the rover follows it. Use a clear room with cushions as rocks, and see how many tries it takes to reach a target.
myth: Mars is red, so it must be a hot planet.
Mars is red because its dust is full of iron oxide, the same stuff as rust. It is actually freezing, with an average temperature of about −60 °C.

sec.t:
The newest rovers are careful drivers. NASA's Perseverance takes pictures, builds a 3D map of the ground, picks a route and checks it again as it moves. It is slow on purpose. Its top speed is about 150 m an hour, slower than a walking tortoise. A stuck rover is a disaster, because there is no tow truck on Mars.

These are the same problems that [[@self-driving|self-driving cars]] on Earth face, with one big difference. A Mars rover can't stop and ask for help.

Perseverance landed in February 2021 in Jezero Crater, which held a lake billions of years ago. Rivers once flowed into it and dropped mud and sand, the kind of place where tiny living things might have left traces. The rover is about the size of a car and runs on a nuclear battery that keeps it powered day and night.

It drills into rocks and seals cores the size of a piece of chalk inside metal tubes. Plans to bring those samples to Earth are still being worked out. It also carries microphones, and has recorded the sound of Martian wind.

Perseverance carried a small helicopter called Ingenuity, which weighed under 2 kg. Mars's air is about one hundredth as thick as Earth's, so its blades had to spin very fast, around 2,400 times a minute. In April 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. It was planned to fly five times. It flew 72 times before a damaged blade grounded it in 2024.

Getting a rover onto Mars safely is a challenge of its own. Curiosity and Perseverance came down using a heat shield, a parachute, rockets, and finally a "sky crane" that lowered each rover on cables and then flew away. Engineers called the last stretch the "seven minutes of terror", because it all had to happen automatically.

India reached Mars too. [[@isro-missions|Mangalyaan]] went into [[orbit|orbit]] in 2014, on its first try, and studied the planet from above. Rovers see Mars from the ground, including its strange blue [[@mars-sky|sunsets]].

text: Horses changed human history more than almost any other animal. Once people learned to ride them and harness them to wheels, they could travel, trade, farm and fight over much larger distances. News, goods, ideas and armies suddenly moved at the speed of a gallop.

Horses carried the Mongols across Asia, pulled chariots in ancient India and Egypt, hauled ploughs on European farms and carried the mail across the American West. For thousands of years, a strong horse was like a car, a tractor and a tank in one. Only in the last hundred years did engines take over most of their work.

st.prompt: Why did James Watt invent the unit called "horsepower" in the 1700s?

options.t: To show buyers how many horses his steam engine could replace
To measure how fast racehorses ran
To count horses in an army

st.reveal: Mines and mills used horses to turn pumps and wheels. Watt wanted a simple way to compare his steam engines with the animals customers already knew. One horsepower became a standard measure of work, and car engines are still rated in it today.

n.certNote: Scientists agree horses were tamed on the grasslands of Eurasia, but they still debate exactly when and where. A 2021 DNA study traced today's domestic horses to the steppes of southern Russia about 4,200 years ago, while older finds in Kazakhstan show people working with horses even earlier.

myth: The wild mustangs of the American West are really wild horses.

Mustangs are feral, descended from tame horses that escaped or were set free, many from Spanish stock. Przewalski's horse of Central Asia, which nearly died out and has been brought back to Mongolia, was long called the last wild horse never tamed by people. A 2018 DNA study suggests even its ancestors were once kept by people at Botai.

sec.t:
The horse family began in North America about 55 million years ago. The first ancestor was about the size of a small dog, with several toes on each foot, living in forests and eating leaves. Over millions of years, as grasslands spread, horses grew bigger and faster, and their toes shrank to a single hoof. It is one of the best-known examples of [[evolution|evolution]] in [[fossil|fossils]].

Horses crossed into Asia over a land bridge that once joined Alaska and Siberia. Then, about 10,000 years ago, they died out in the Americas, perhaps because of [[climate|climate]] change and hunting. They survived only in Asia, Europe and Africa.

Horses play a big part in early Indian texts. The Rigveda praises them, and kings performed a ceremony called the Ashvamedha, involving a horse. In the epics, Krishna drives Arjuna's chariot pulled by white horses.

India's hot climate wasn't ideal for breeding big warhorses, so for centuries rulers imported fine horses from Central Asia and Arabia, often by sea through ports on the west coast. India also bred its own. The Marwari horse of Rajasthan and the Kathiawari of Gujarat have ears that curl inward until the tips nearly touch. [[@rajputs|Rajput]] warriors prized them, and the story of Maharana Pratap's horse Chetak is still told today.

In the 1200s, [[@mongols|Mongol]] riders built the largest land [[empire|empire]] in history. Each soldier often had several horses, switching when one tired, so armies could cover great distances in a day. They used a relay system of horse stations to carry messages across the empire.

Horses also changed farming. Heavy horses pulling iron ploughs could break tough soil, and in Europe they slowly replaced slower oxen in many areas. More food meant bigger towns.

When the Spanish arrived in the Americas from the 1490s, they brought horses back to the land where the family began. Some escaped. Over the next two centuries, [[@native-nations|nations of the Great Plains]], such as the Comanche and Lakota, became superb riders. Horses let them hunt bison far more easily and travel widely.

In 1860 and 1861, riders of the Pony Express carried mail across the American West in about ten days, swapping horses at stations. The [[telegraph|telegraph]] soon replaced them, and later cars and tractors replaced most working horses. Today, horses race, jump, pull tongas in some Indian towns and still help herders and farmers around the world.

text: Plastics are made of [[polymer|polymers]]. A polymer is a giant [[molecule|molecule]] made of small units, called monomers, joined end to end in a long chain, like beads on a necklace. A single chain can contain thousands of units.

Most plastics start with oil or natural gas. At chemical plants, these are broken into small molecules. One of the most common is ethylene, a gas. Under the right heat, pressure and help from other chemicals, ethylene molecules link up into long chains called polyethylene, or polythene. That's the plastic in carry bags, milk pouches and many bottles.

By choosing different starting molecules and adding colours or softeners, chemists can make plastics that are clear or coloured, soft or hard, stretchy or stiff. That flexibility is why plastic is used for almost everything.

options.t: Oil and natural gas

st.reveal: Most plastic starts as chemicals taken from oil and natural gas. These small molecules are joined into very long chains. A few newer plastics are made from plants like sugarcane or maize, but they are still a small share.

Then link some chains to each other with extra clips and see how much stiffer the heap becomes. That's similar to how some plastics are soft and stretchy while others are hard.
myth: Plastic labelled biodegradable will rot away anywhere, like food scraps.
Many biodegradable plastics only break down properly in industrial composting plants, which are hot and carefully controlled. In the sea or a landfill, they can last for years.
facts: polymers, long chains of repeating units

sec.t:
Picture a bowl of cooked noodles. The noodles slide past each other, but they also tangle. Polymer chains behave a bit like that, which is why many plastics can bend and stretch without breaking.

In some plastics, the chains are only tangled, not tied together. Heat them and they soften and can be moulded again. These are called thermoplastics, and they include the plastics in most bottles and boxes. In others, the chains are linked to each other by strong cross-bonds. Once set, they won't melt. These are used for things like [[@fuses-switches|electrical switches]] and pan handles.

Plastic production took off after [[@world-war-two|World War Two]]. Nylon stockings, plastic toys, polythene bags and soft drink bottles became normal within a few decades. Today the world makes more than 400 million tonnes of plastic a year, close to the combined weight of every person on Earth.

Plastic is light, cheap, [[@raincoats-waterproof|waterproof]] and strong. It keeps medicines clean, food fresh and electrical wires safe. Car makers use it to make vehicles lighter, so they use less fuel. Hospitals rely on it for syringes, drips and gloves that are used once and thrown away, which helps stop germs spreading from one patient to another.

The same toughness causes problems. Most plastics don't rot. Instead, sunlight and waves break them into smaller and smaller pieces called [[microplastic|microplastics]], which have been found in the deepest oceans, on mountain tops and in the bodies of animals. Much of the plastic that escapes into rivers ends up as [[@ocean-plastic|ocean plastic]].

Only a small share of plastic has ever been [[@recycling|recycled]]. Scientists are working on plastics made from plants, ones that break down more easily, and better ways to recycle them. In 2022, India banned a list of single-use plastic items, including plastic straws, plastic cutlery and thin carry bags.

text: The patterns on a tyre, called the tread, are mainly there to deal with water. When a road is wet, the grooves give water somewhere to go, so the rubber can still touch the road. Without them, a tyre could float on a thin layer of water and lose its grip.
Treads also help on mud, gravel and snow, where the blocks of rubber bite into the ground. That's why a tractor tyre looks so different from a racing car tyre. Each pattern is designed for a job.

Your shoes work the same way. Trainers and school shoes have grooved soles for the same reason, so you don't slip on a wet bathroom floor or a muddy playground. A smooth leather sole feels fine on carpet and skids on a rainy pavement.

options.t: More rubber touches the road, giving more grip

myth: Tyres are black because rubber is naturally black.
Natural rubber from trees is milky white or pale yellow. Tyres are black because makers add carbon black, a fine soot that makes the rubber stronger and helps it last longer.

sec.t:
Picture a tyre rolling over a wet road. Water gets trapped between the rubber and the road. The tread's grooves act like drains, squirting that water out to the sides and back.

If the grooves can't clear the water fast enough, the tyre starts riding on top of it. This is called aquaplaning, or hydroplaning in the US. The steering suddenly feels light and the brakes do little, because the tyre has almost no [[@friction|friction]] with the road. It's most dangerous at high speed on roads flooded by a [[@monsoon|monsoon]] downpour.

On a dry track, grooves are a waste. Every groove means less rubber touching the road. So [[@formula-one|Formula One]] cars use slicks, smooth tyres with no tread, when it's dry. They grip so hard that they get hot and sticky, almost like chewing gum.

If it starts to rain, teams rush the cars into the pits and swap to grooved wet-weather tyres. A slick on a wet track would aquaplane almost at once.

sec.h: From cushions of air to black rubber
sec.t:
In 1845 a Scottish engineer, Robert William Thomson, patented a tyre filled with air, but it didn't catch on. In 1888 John Boyd Dunlop, a vet in Belfast, made air-filled tyres for his son's tricycle to give a smoother ride. They soon spread to [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]] and then cars.

Early rubber tyres were pale. Makers found that mixing in carbon black, a fine soot, made rubber much tougher. Tyres have been black ever since. In India, the company MRF started in 1946 by making toy balloons in Madras, now Chennai, before it moved on to tyres.

Every time you drive, a tiny layer of rubber wears away. As the tread gets shallower, the grooves can't carry as much water. Many countries, including the UK and most of Europe, set a legal minimum tread depth of 1.6 millimetres, about the thickness of a coin. Most US states use a similar limit.

Many tyres have small bars, called wear indicators, moulded into the bottom of the grooves. When the tread wears down level with them, it's time for new tyres. Worn tyres take much longer to stop on a wet road, even with good [[@brakes|brakes]].

text: Jazz grew up in [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]], in the southern USA, around 1900. It was created mainly by African American musicians, who mixed several kinds of music: [[@blues|the blues]], ragtime piano, brass band marches, church spirituals and the [[rhythm|rhythms]] of the Caribbean.

The result had a bouncy, swinging feel, with notes landing off the beat. Above all, jazz musicians improvised. They made up new melodies on the spot, around a familiar tune, so no two performances were exactly the same. From New Orleans, jazz spread across America and then the world.

st.reveal: Jazz grew up in New Orleans around 1900. Chicago and New York became important later, when musicians moved north and jazz spread through records and radio.

sec.t:
New Orleans was a port city with French, Spanish, African and Caribbean influences. Brass bands played at [[@parades|parades]], picnics and funerals, slow on the way to the cemetery and joyful on the way back.

In this mix, musicians began to play together in a new way. A trumpet led the tune, a clarinet wove around it, and a trombone added low slides beneath, all improvising at once over drums and bass. In 1917, a band made the first jazz record, and the new sound reached homes across the country.

Louis Armstrong, born in New Orleans in 1901, changed jazz. His trumpet solos were bold, inventive and full of feeling. He showed that one player stepping forward to improvise could be the most exciting part of a song. He also sang in a gravelly voice and helped make "scat" singing popular, using made-up [[syllable|syllables]] instead of words.

Many Black musicians, like Armstrong, moved north to cities such as [[@chicago|Chicago]] and New York during the Great Migration, looking for work and escaping unfair laws in the South. Jazz went with them.

In the 1930s, big bands led by musicians like Duke Ellington played swing music for dancing across America. In the 1940s, younger players invented bebop: fast, complex and made for listening. Later came cool jazz, Latin jazz and jazz mixed with rock.

All this happened while Black Americans faced segregation, and jazz musicians often could not stay in the hotels where they performed. Their fight for fairness was part of the wider [[@civil-rights|civil rights]] story.

Jazz reached India in the 1920s and 1930s. African American musicians, including the pianist Teddy Weatherford, played at the Taj Mahal Hotel in Bombay, now Mumbai. Musicians from [[@goa|Goa]], many trained in church music, picked up jazz quickly and played in dance halls.

Some of these Goan musicians later worked as arrangers for Hindi films. They brought jazz trumpets, saxophones and swing rhythms into many [[@bollywood-music|Bollywood songs]] of the 1950s and 1960s. In 1963, Duke Ellington's [[@orchestra|orchestra]] toured India, and audiences heard the music from its source.

text: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906) was a painter from Kerala who changed how Indians pictured their gods, goddesses and heroes. He used oil paint and the realistic style of European art, but he painted Indian stories, Indian faces and Indian clothes.

His paintings of scenes from the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] and [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] made gods look like real people you might meet. Then he did something unusual for an artist. He opened a printing press and sold cheap copies of his pictures. They spread to homes, shops and [[@calendars|calendars]] across India, and many images of gods that families pray to today follow his style.

st.prompt: What new kind of paint did Ravi Varma become famous for using in India?

options.t: Oil paint, which European artists had used for centuries
Spray paint from cans

st.reveal: Oil paint dries slowly, so artists can blend colours smoothly and paint soft skin, shining silk and glowing light. Few Indian painters used it in his time, and Ravi Varma largely taught himself.

sec.h: A boy who drew on palace walls
sec.t:
Ravi Varma was born in Kilimanoor, a small town in the kingdom of Travancore, in what is now [[@kerala|Kerala]]. His family was connected to the royal family. As a child he is said to have drawn on walls with charcoal, and an uncle who was a painter encouraged him.

At the Travancore palace he saw European paintings and watched a visiting British portrait painter work in oils. Oil paint was rare in India then. Ravi Varma had little formal training, so he taught himself to mix colours and use the medium, through years of practice.

In 1894 Ravi Varma opened a press near Bombay to print [[lithograph|lithographs]] of his paintings. In his day, temple images were mostly carved statues inside temples, and fine paintings belonged to kings. Suddenly, a family could buy a colourful print of Lakshmi, Saraswati or Krishna for a small price.

The prints sold in huge numbers. They decorated homes, shops and later calendars and matchboxes. Like the [[@printing-press|printing press]] that spread books in Europe, his press spread pictures, and his way of showing the gods became the way millions imagined them.

Ravi Varma was hugely popular in his lifetime and is often called the father of modern Indian art. Still, not everyone admired him. Some later artists and critics felt he copied European styles too closely, making Indian gods look like figures from Western theatre. They wanted an art that grew from Indian traditions such as Mughal painting or temple [[mural|murals]].

His pictures have also been criticised for showing only one idea of beauty, mostly fair-skinned and upper-class. Supporters reply that he made art available to ordinary people for the first time, which few painters before him had done.

Ravi Varma died in 1906. His influence did not. The look of early Indian films, with gods in glittering crowns and painted backdrops, borrowed from his prints. Many of India's early [[@bollywood|film-makers]] grew up surrounded by his pictures. More than a century later, his images still appear on posters and in TV serials about the epics, and the government named an award for artists after him in Kerala.

text: Christmas is the Christian festival that celebrates the birth of Jesus. Most churches mark it on 25 December, with special services, carols, decorations and family meals. It has also become a holiday enjoyed by many people who are not Christian.

Its customs come from many places and times. The date was fixed in Rome in the 300s. Christmas trees came from [[@germany|Germany]], cards from Victorian London, and much of today's Santa Claus from the USA in the 1800s. Over centuries, each country has added its own food, songs and traditions.

He invented the postage stamp
He hired a team of letter writers

st.reveal: Cole asked an artist to design a card with a festive picture and a short greeting, and had about a thousand printed. Within a few decades, sending Christmas cards had become a tradition in Britain and the USA.

d.try: Design your own greeting card for any festival your family celebrates. Fold a sheet of paper, draw a picture on the front and write a short message inside. Make a few copies by tracing over the first one, and give them to neighbours or relatives.
myth: Coca-Cola invented Santa Claus's red suit.
Santa was often shown in red long before Coca-Cola's famous advertisements of the 1930s. The adverts did help fix the image of a big, jolly Santa in red and white in many people's minds.
facts: the birth of Jesus, for Christians

sec.t:
The Bible does not say on what day Jesus was born. The earliest record of a Christmas celebration on 25 December comes from a Roman calendar for the year 336 CE.

Historians have different ideas about why that day was chosen. Some think it was meant to replace Roman winter festivals held around the same time. Others point to early Christian calculations about Jesus's life. Many Orthodox churches still follow the older Julian [[@calendars|calendar]], so their 25 December falls on what most of the world calls [[@oddity-calendar-missing-days|7 January]].

Santa Claus began with Saint Nicholas, a bishop who lived in Myra, in what is now Turkey, in the 300s. Many stories describe him as kind and generous to the poor. In the Netherlands, his feast became a day for children's gifts, and his Dutch name, Sinterklaas, later became Santa Claus.

Dutch settlers brought the custom to New York. In 1823, an American poem, "A Visit from St. Nicholas", described Santa landing on rooftops with eight reindeer. From the 1860s, the cartoonist Thomas Nast drew Santa as a round, bearded man for a popular magazine, and that picture stuck.

About 2 to 3 per cent of Indians are Christian, which is still millions of people. Christmas, sometimes called Bada Din, "the big day", is a national holiday. In [[@goa|Goa]] and Kerala, churches hold midnight Mass and homes hang paper star lanterns.

In Nagaland, Mizoram and Meghalaya, where most people are Christian, whole towns decorate for weeks, as [[@northeast-india|northeast India]] describes. In [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], Park Street is strung with lights, and bakeries sell rich plum cake. Many families of every faith buy a cake or visit the lights.

In the United States, Christmas has been a [[federal|federal]] holiday since 1870. Families decorate trees, hang stockings and leave cookies and milk for Santa. Cities put up giant trees, such as the one at New York's Rockefeller Center, lit every year since the 1930s.

For many families, Christmas is a religious celebration; for others, it is mostly a time for family, food and giving. Both kinds of celebration sit side by side. The days that follow lead straight into the [[@new-year|New Year]], which is why late December is holiday season in so many countries.

text: Lionel Messi of [[@argentina|Argentina]] and Cristiano Ronaldo of Portugal are two of the greatest footballers ever. From 2008 to 2023 they won the Ballon d'Or, the most famous award for the world's best player, 13 times between them. Both scored hundreds of goals for their clubs and countries and broke record after record.

They are very different. Messi is small and quiet, with close dribbling and clever passes. Ronaldo is tall and powerful, a great header of the ball and a fierce athlete. Fans love to argue about which one is better, and the debate shows no sign of ending.

sec.h: Messi: the small boy from Rosario
sec.t:
Messi was born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1987. He was obviously gifted, but at about 10 doctors found he did not produce enough growth [[@hormones|hormone]]. The treatment was expensive. FC Barcelona offered to help, and at 13 he moved to [[@spain|Spain]] with his family.

He grew to about 1.70 metres. At Barcelona he became the club's all-time top scorer, and won the Champions League four times. His low centre of [[gravity|gravity]] let him change direction almost instantly, which made him very hard to tackle.

sec.h: Ronaldo: the boy from an island

sec.t:
From 2009 to 2018 Ronaldo played for Real Madrid while Messi played for Barcelona. Their matches, called El Clásico, became some of the most-watched club games in the world. Each season one of them seemed to break a scoring record set by the other.

Messi won the Ballon d'Or a record eight times, the last in 2023. Ronaldo won it five times. Many experts say having such a rival pushed both to be better. In the 2011–12 season Messi scored 73 goals for Barcelona in all competitions, and in 2012 he scored 91 goals in a calendar year, a world record at the time.

For years, critics said Messi could not win for Argentina. He lost a World Cup final in 2014 and several Copa América finals. Then he won the Copa América in 2021 and [[@pop-world-cup-trophy|the World Cup]] in Qatar in 2022, scoring twice in a thrilling final against France.

Ronaldo led Portugal to their first major trophy at Euro 2016, even though he was injured early in the final and cheered from the side. He became the first man to score at five World Cups.

Both are hugely popular online. Ronaldo has more Instagram followers than any other person, and Messi is not far behind. Their [[@social-media|social media]] posts reach more people than many TV channels.

In 2023 Messi joined Inter [[@miami|Miami]] in the USA, and Ronaldo moved to Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia. Indian fans have their own memories: Messi played for Argentina at Kolkata's Salt Lake Stadium in 2011, in a friendly against Venezuela, and a huge crowd came to watch.

text: A giant stadium is a bowl of seats wrapped around a field. Almost every part of it is designed for one job: letting tens of thousands of people see clearly and get in and out safely.

Builders start with the ground. Huge foundations, often concrete piles driven deep into the soil, carry the weight. Then come the stands, built from steel frames or [[@cement-concrete|concrete]] sections, often made in factories and lifted into place by cranes. The seats rise steeply so every row can see over the one in front.
Last comes the roof, the hardest part. It has to cover the crowd without a single pillar in the way.

st.reveal: A cantilever roof is held down at the back and sticks out over the seats, like a diving board. That way no column blocks anyone's view of the pitch.

sec.t:
A roof over a crowd is like a huge lid. Pillars would hold it up easily, but they'd block the view. So engineers use cantilevers: roofs held down firmly at the back of the stand that stick out over the seats like a diving board. Cables or steel trusses carry the weight back to strong supports behind the crowd.

London's Wembley Stadium hangs part of its roof from a steel arch 133 metres high, which you can see from miles away. Some stadiums in the USA have roofs that slide open and shut in good or bad weather.

The [[@ahmedabad|Narendra Modi Stadium]] in Ahmedabad, rebuilt and reopened in 2021, can seat about 1,32,000 people, making it the largest cricket stadium in the world. Its roof is held up so that no pillars stand in front of the seats.

In the USA, the biggest is Michigan Stadium, known as "The Big House", with over 1,07,000 seats. Kolkata's Eden Gardens, one of India's oldest grounds, has hosted [[@cricket-history|cricket]] since the 1860s.

Grass needs sunlight, air and water, and a stadium's walls and roof block much of that. Groundstaff use giant grow lamps on wheels to light the turf at night, and fans under the field to move air through the soil.

Many big grounds now use hybrid grass. Machines stitch millions of plastic fibres deep into the soil, and the grass roots wrap around them. The pitch looks and plays like natural grass but doesn't tear up as easily when players slide or stop suddenly. At a few stadiums, like the one in Glendale, Arizona, the whole grass pitch sits on a giant tray that rolls outside to soak up the sunshine.

Engineers plan exits as carefully as seats. In many countries, safety rules say a full stand should be able to empty within a few minutes in an emergency. That means wide stairways, many gates and clear signs. Ramps, lifts and wheelchair spaces with clear views help disabled fans and older visitors too. After big events, it can still take an hour for trains and roads to clear.

Building a stadium takes years and teams of [[@jobs-engineer|engineers]], architects and thousands of workers. The best ones feel simple when you're inside: you find your seat, look out, and the whole field is right in front of you.

text: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, often called Babasaheb, was a lawyer, economist, writer and political leader. He is best known for leading the committee that drafted India's [[@constitution|Constitution]], the rulebook the whole country runs on.

He was born into a community that the [[@caste-history|caste system]] treated as "untouchable". People from his community were kept out of temples, wells and many schools. Ambedkar spent his life fighting this unfairness. He wanted an India where every person had the same rights, whatever family they were born into.

sec.t:
Ambedkar was born in 1891 in Mhow, an army town in central India, where his father served in the British Indian Army. At school he had to sit apart from other children, sometimes on a sack he brought from home. He later wrote that he could only drink water if the school's peon poured it for him. When the peon was away, he went thirsty.

He studied anyway, and kept studying. He became one of the first in his community to finish college, at Elphinstone College in Bombay.

With a scholarship from the ruler of Baroda, Ambedkar went to Columbia University in [[@new-york|New York]] in 1913. Away from the caste rules of home, he could live, eat and study alongside anyone. He then studied at the [[@london|London]] School of Economics and trained as a barrister.

By the 1920s he had doctorates from both universities. He came home to practise law, teach and start [[@newspapers|newspapers]] that spoke for oppressed communities. One of them, *Mooknayak*, means "leader of the voiceless". He also wrote on money and banking, and his ideas fed into discussions that led to the Reserve Bank of India.

His message to his followers was short: educate, agitate, organise.

In 1927 he led the Mahad Satyagraha, when thousands of people drank from a public tank they had been barred from. Later campaigns demanded entry to temples.

Ambedkar and [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] both opposed untouchability, but they disagreed sharply on how to end it. In 1932 Ambedkar wanted separate electorates, so oppressed communities could choose their own representatives. Gandhi went on a fast against the idea. The two signed the Poona Pact, which [[@reservation-india|reserved seats]] for these communities instead. Historians still discuss that moment, and both men's views have supporters.

Late in life Ambedkar turned to the teachings of the [[@buddha|Buddha]], which he saw as a path of equality and reason. On 14 October 1956, in Nagpur, he became a Buddhist along with several hundred thousand followers. The place is now called Deekshabhoomi.

He died less than two months later, on 6 December 1956. Every year on that date, huge crowds gather at Chaityabhoomi in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], where he was cremated. India awarded him its highest honour, the Bharat Ratna, in 1990. His birthday, 14 April, is celebrated across India, and his statues, often holding a copy of the Constitution, stand in towns and villages everywhere.

text: For more than 2,000 years, [[@ancient-china|China]] was ruled by emperors. The last [[dynasty|dynasty]], the Qing, grew weak in the 1800s after losing wars to foreign powers. In 1911 a revolt broke out, and in early 1912 the boy emperor Puyi gave up the throne. China became a [[republic|republic]].

The republic struggled. Generals fought over [[territory|territory]], Japan invaded, and two parties, the Nationalists and the Communists, battled for control. In 1949 the Communists under Mao Zedong won, and founded the People's Republic of China. Much of what China is today grew out of those decades of upheaval.

sec.t:
By 1900 many Chinese people blamed the Qing for letting foreign countries push China around, ever since the [[@opium-wars|Opium Wars]]. A doctor named Sun Yat-sen spent years abroad raising money for a revolution, including from Chinese workers in America.

On 10 October 1911, soldiers in the city of Wuchang rebelled. Province after province joined them. Sun became the first president of the new Republic of China on 1 January 1912, and Puyi, aged six, gave up his throne a few weeks later. He was allowed to keep living in the [[@forbidden-city|Forbidden City]] for a while, an emperor with no [[empire|empire]].

Sun Yat-sen's own time in charge was short, but his ideas lasted. Today he is honoured both in mainland China and in Taiwan, two governments that agree on very little else. His portrait hangs in Tiananmen Square every year on National Day.

sec.h: War with Japan, then civil war
sec.t:
Japan invaded northern China in 1931 and launched a full war in 1937. Millions died. The Nationalists and Communists fought Japan, sometimes side by side, while still distrusting each other. When Japan was defeated in 1945, their civil war began again.

The Communists won the support of many poor farmers and gained ground. On 1 October 1949 Mao announced the People's Republic from the Tiananmen gate in Beijing. Chiang's government retreated to the island of Taiwan, where the Republic of China continued. As the [[@cold-war|Cold War]] set in, the United States backed Chiang's government and the Soviet Union backed Mao's. How Taiwan relates to mainland China is still disputed today.

Mao's rule brought land reform, more schools and better basic health care. It also brought disasters. The Great Leap Forward, a rushed plan to industrialise from 1958, led to a [[famine|famine]] in which tens of millions of people died. The Cultural Revolution, from 1966, closed many schools and turned students against teachers and parents.

After Mao died in 1976, a new leader, Deng Xiaoping, changed course. From 1978 China opened to foreign trade and let people run businesses. The country grew into one of the world's largest [[economy|economies]], though the Communist Party still holds firm control. Today China makes a large share of the world's phones, toys and clothes.

text: For more than 200 years, Japan was ruled by military leaders called shoguns, and the emperor had little real power. Foreign trade was tightly controlled, and society was split into fixed classes, with [[@samurai|samurai]] warriors near the top.

Then, in 1853, American warships arrived and forced Japan to open its ports. Young leaders decided Japan must change fast or be pushed around like China had been. In 1868 they took power in the name of the teenage Emperor Meiji. Over the next four decades they rebuilt the country, borrowing ideas from the West and shaping them to suit Japan.

st.prompt: When the Meiji government built a modern silk factory at Tomioka in 1872, how did it learn to run the new machines?

options.t: It hired an expert from France and copied French equipment
It invented every machine from scratch in secret
It sent all the workers to study in China

st.reveal: Japan hired foreign experts for many new projects. At Tomioka a French engineer helped set up the mill, and young Japanese women trained there, then taught the methods in other factories.

myth: Japan was completely cut off from the world until 1853.

Japan limited foreign contact for over 200 years, but never shut it off entirely. Dutch and Chinese traders kept doing business at Nagasaki, and Japanese scholars studied European books on medicine and science.

sec.t:
In July 1853 four American ships steamed into the bay near Edo, today's [[@tokyo|Tokyo]]. Two of them belched black smoke from their coal engines, and the Japanese called them the "black ships". Commodore Matthew Perry demanded that Japan trade with the United States.

Japan's leaders knew what had happened next door. In the [[@opium-wars|Opium Wars]], Britain had beaten China and seized Hong Kong. Japan signed [[treaty|treaties]] with the Americans and Europeans, but many people felt shamed, and the old shogun government began to crumble.

sec.h: A new emperor and a new capital

sec.t:
Japan sent students abroad and invited foreign experts in. In 1872 the first railway opened between Tokyo and Yokohama, a ride of under an hour that had taken most of a day on foot. In the same year, the government ordered schools for all children, girls as well as boys.

Factories came next. The Tomioka Silk Mill, opened in 1872, used French machines to reel [[@silk|silk]] thread. Silk became one of Japan's biggest [[export|exports]] and paid for much of the modernising. The mill is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Change reached the dinner table and the wardrobe too. Buddhist custom had discouraged eating meat for centuries, but in 1872 the palace let it be known that the emperor ate beef. Officials started wearing Western suits, and the emperor was photographed in a military uniform rather than court robes.

Even time changed. At the end of 1872 Japan dropped its old moon-based [[@oddity-calendar-missing-days|calendar]] for the one used in Europe. The switch was so sudden that the third day of the twelfth month simply became 1 January 1873, and nearly a month vanished from the year.
In 1889 Japan adopted a written [[constitution|constitution]] with an elected [[parliament|parliament]], though the emperor kept wide powers and only a small share of men could vote.

By 1900 Japan had a modern army and navy. It defeated China in 1895 and Russia in 1905. It was the first time in modern history that an Asian country beat a European great power in a major war, and the news thrilled people across Asia. [[@nehru|Jawaharlal Nehru]], then a schoolboy in India, later wrote of the excitement he felt.

But Japan also built an [[empire|empire]] of its own. It took Taiwan in 1895 and made Korea a colony in 1910, ruling both harshly. When Emperor Meiji died in 1912, Japan was rich and strong, and set on a path that would lead to [[@world-war-two|World War Two]].

text: The Vijayanagara Empire was a great south Indian kingdom that lasted from 1336 to the 1600s. At its height it covered most of the land south of the Krishna river, across today's Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu.

Its capital, Vijayanagara, meaning "city of victory", stood on the Tungabhadra river. Its ruins are now known as [[@hampi|Hampi]]. The [[empire|empire]] grew rich from farming, temple [[economy|economies]] and trade in [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]], spices and gems, and it bought war horses from overseas. Its kings supported temples, poets and festivals in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. After a heavy defeat at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, the capital was abandoned.

st.prompt: Vijayanagara's kings bought thousands of horses every year. Where did most of them come from?

options.t: Across the sea, from Arabia and Persia
Horse farms in the Western Ghats
Wild herds caught in the Thar Desert

st.reveal: Good war horses did not breed well in south India's climate. So kings imported them by ship from Arabia and Persia, through ports such as Goa and Bhatkal, paying huge sums. Controlling the horse trade was a key reason for Vijayanagara's deals with the Portuguese.

n.certNote: The empire's history after about 1400 is well recorded. Its founding story is partly legend, and historians disagree about the founders' early lives and loyalties.

The capital never recovered, but the dynasty carried on from new capitals such as Penukonda and Chandragiri for almost another century.

sec.h: Two brothers and a city of victory
sec.t:
The usual story says two brothers, Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family, founded the kingdom in 1336. They had served local rulers who were swept aside when armies of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] raided the south.

Legend adds that a sage named Vidyaranya guided them, and that they once saw a hare turn and chase hunting dogs at the spot where they built their city. Historians treat that tale with caution. The brothers' early careers, and whether they spoke Kannada or Telugu, are still argued about.

sec.h: A city as big as Rome
sec.t:
Visitors were stunned. The Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq came in 1443 and described seven rings of walls. A Portuguese trader named Domingo Paes, who visited around 1520, wrote that the city was as large as Rome and very beautiful.

Paes described markets piled with rice, fruit, cloth and [[@spices|spices]], and stalls selling [[@pearls|pearls]], rubies and diamonds. He also watched the Mahanavami festival, when the king sat on a great stone platform to watch wrestling, dancing and parades of elephants and horses. That platform still stands at Hampi.

Cavalry won wars in [[medieval|medieval]] India, but good war horses did not thrive in the south. So Vijayanagara imported thousands every year from Arabia and Persia, landing them at west coast ports.

After the Portuguese took [[@goa|Goa]] in 1510, they became important horse traders. Krishnadevaraya kept friendly terms with them so the horses would keep coming. Trade kept the empire strong as much as conquest did. Portuguese writers such as Fernão Nunes, who lived in the city in the 1530s, left detailed accounts of its kings, armies and customs, which historians still rely on.

In 1565, an alliance of four Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara's army near Talikota, far to the north of the capital. The regent, Aliya Rama Raya, was killed.

With its army gone, the city had no defence. It was looted and burned over several months, and its people left. An Italian traveller who passed through soon afterwards found it empty. The [[dynasty|dynasty]] carried on from smaller capitals, and the old city's [[granite|granite]] temples and walls were left to the monkeys, the boulders and, much later, the archaeologists.

text: The Seven Wonders of the World began as a list of must-see sights made by Greek writers over 2,000 years ago. It was a bit like a traveller's guidebook. The Greeks called them "theamata", which means "things to be seen", and they picked buildings and statues around the eastern Mediterranean, the part of the world they knew.

The usual list starts with the Great Pyramid of Giza and the Hanging Gardens of Babylon. Then come the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. Only the pyramid survives. In 2007, a public vote picked a "new" seven, which includes India's [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]].

st.prompt: Only one of the seven ancient wonders is still standing today. Which one?

options.t: The Great Pyramid of Giza
The Colossus of Rhodes
The Lighthouse of Alexandria

st.reveal: The Great Pyramid, built around 4,500 years ago, is the oldest wonder and the only survivor. The Colossus fell in an earthquake after about 50 years, and the Lighthouse was ruined by earthquakes in the Middle Ages.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Seven Wonders of the World.
Clayton P. and Price M. (eds) (1988) The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Routledge.
n.certNote: The ancient list was never fixed, and different writers named different wonders. Historians still debate whether the Hanging Gardens of Babylon existed at all. The 2007 "New Seven Wonders" came from a public vote, not from experts.

myth: There is one official list of the Seven Wonders of the World.
Ancient writers made several different lists. The famous 2007 list came from a vote organised by a private foundation, and UNESCO did not take part. There is no single official list.
facts: the Great Pyramid, about 146 m when built

sec.t:
The others are gone. The Statue of Zeus was a giant seated figure covered in ivory and gold. The Temple of Artemis was burned down, rebuilt and finally destroyed. The tomb of Mausolus, a ruler in what is now Turkey, was so grand that its name gave us the word "[[mausoleum|mausoleum]]".

The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze statue of the sun god, about 33 m tall, roughly as high as a ten-storey building. It stood for only around 50 years before an earthquake toppled it. The Lighthouse of Alexandria guided ships into Egypt's busy harbour with a fire at the top, as you can read in [[@lighthouses|lighthouses]].

sec.h: The gardens that may not have existed
sec.t:
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, in what is now Iraq, are said to have been terraces of trees and flowers watered by clever machines. The trouble is that no Babylonian writing describes them, and [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] have not found them.

Some historians think the gardens were legendary. Others think they were real but stood in a different city, Nineveh, built by an Assyrian king. So one of the world's most famous wonders may be the one we know least about.

In 2007, a Swiss-based foundation ran a worldwide vote by internet and phone. The winners were the [[@great-wall|Great Wall]] of China, [[@petra|Petra]] in Jordan and [[@christ-redeemer|Christ the Redeemer]] in Brazil. Joining them were [[@inca-machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]] in [[@peru|Peru]], Chichén Itzá in Mexico, the [[@colosseum|Colosseum]] in Rome and the Taj Mahal in India. The Great Pyramid was given an honorary place.

Countries with big populations and keen campaigns had an advantage, so the list says as much about popularity as about greatness. UNESCO, which looks after World Heritage Sites, kept its distance from the vote.

People argue about what is missing. Many would add [[@angkor-wat|Angkor Wat]] in Cambodia, the [[@ellora-kailasa|Kailasa temple]] at Ellora carved down into a single rock, or modern wonders like the [[@panama-canal|Panama Canal]].

Every list leaves something out. That is part of why people keep making new ones.

text: Venice sits in a shallow [[lagoon|lagoon]] on the north-east coast of Italy, spread across about 118 small islands. The ground was soft mud, which could not hold up heavy stone buildings. So the Venetians drove millions of wooden poles straight down through the mud, packed them tightly together, and laid platforms of wood and stone on top. Then they built palaces, churches and houses on those platforms.
Instead of streets, much of Venice has canals, about 150 of them, crossed by around 400 [[@bridges|bridges]]. There are no cars in the old city. People walk, or travel by boat.

st.prompt: Venice stands on wooden poles sunk into mud. Why haven't they rotted away?

options.t: The mud has almost no oxygen, so rot can't start
They were painted with a special varnish
Salt water slowly turned them into stone

st.reveal: Fungi and bacteria that rot wood need oxygen. Packed in wet mud and clay, the poles get almost none. Over centuries, minerals from the water have also seeped into the wood and helped harden it.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Venice and its Lagoon.

myth: Venice floats on rafts or platforms on the water.
Venice does not float. Its buildings stand on wooden poles driven down through soft mud into firmer clay below. Stone platforms on top of the poles hold up the walls.

sec.t:
About 1,500 years ago, the Roman Empire in the west was falling apart and armies swept through northern Italy. People living on the mainland fled to the marshy islands of the lagoon, where the shallow water and mudflats made it hard for attackers to follow. At first they lived as fishers and salt makers.

Over time the scattered villages joined into a city. Venetians learned to manage the lagoon, digging channels and building up the islands.

To build, workers hammered wooden poles, often of oak, alder and larch, deep into the mud. The poles were packed so closely that together they acted like solid ground. The church of Santa Maria della Salute, finished in 1687, rests on more than a million of them.

Wood usually rots, but under Venice it lies in wet mud and clay with almost no oxygen. Without oxygen, the [[fungus|fungi]] and [[bacteria|bacteria]] that cause rot cannot do their work. On top of the poles, builders laid stone from Istria that water can't easily soak into, to protect the brick walls above.

For about 1,100 years Venice was an independent [[republic|republic]], led by an elected ruler called the Doge. Its ships carried silk, spices, glass and salt between Europe, the Middle East and Asia. The traveller [[@marco-polo|Marco Polo]] was a Venetian merchant who journeyed to China in the 1270s.

Venice's [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] made it one of the richest cities in Europe. In 1291, its glassmakers were moved to the island of Murano, partly to protect the city from fires. Murano [[@glass-made|glass]] is still famous today.

{{story:glass-made}}

The republic ended in 1797, when [[@napoleon|Napoleon]]'s army took the city.

The Grand Canal winds through the city like a backwards S, lined with palaces. The Rialto Bridge, built of stone in 1591, crosses it. Gondolas, long thin black boats, are rowed by a gondolier standing at the back with one oar. A gondola is built slightly lopsided, curved more on one side, so it travels straight even though it is rowed from one side only.

Venice floods often, especially in autumn and winter, when high [[@tides|tides]] and winds push water into the lagoon. Venetians call it acqua alta, "high water". In November 2019, water rose about 1.9 m above normal, flooding most of the city. The city is also slowly sinking, while the [[@sea-level-rise|sea level]] is rising.

To fight back, engineers built MOSE, a barrier of 78 giant gates on the seabed at the lagoon's entrances. When a dangerous tide comes, the gates fill with air and rise to hold back the sea. They were first raised in October 2020, and St Mark's Square stayed dry.

Only about 50,000 people now live in the old city, far fewer than in the past, while millions of tourists come each year. Since 2024, day visitors on the busiest days have had to pay a small entry fee to help the city cope with the crowds.

text: Malgudi is an imaginary small town in South India, invented by the writer R. K. Narayan. *Malgudi Days* is one of his collections of short stories, first published in 1943. It is also the name of a much-loved television series based on his stories, first shown on Doordarshan in 1986.

The stories are about ordinary people: a schoolboy, an astrologer, a postman, a snake charmer, a stubborn old man. Nothing very dramatic happens in most of them. Their charm lies in small details, gentle humour and a sharp eye for how people really behave.
For many Indians, the hummed theme tune of the TV series, "ta na na, ta na na na", brings back childhood in a few seconds.

st.prompt: R. K. Narayan said Malgudi first came into his mind as one particular place. What was it?

options.t: A small railway station
A temple on a hill
A school playground

st.reveal: Narayan often said that the town began with an image of a little railway station, and the name Malgudi came with it. The station shows up again and again in his stories, from Swami's adventures to The Guide.

sec.h: A town that grew in books
sec.t:
Malgudi first appeared in Narayan's first novel, *Swami and Friends*, in 1935. It follows Swaminathan, a ten-year-old who hates arithmetic, dodges homework and gets into scrapes with his friends.

Narayan kept returning to Malgudi for the rest of his life, in more than a dozen novels and many short stories. Over the years the town grew. It got a new bank, a cinema, a printing press, a college. Readers watched it change from a sleepy place into a busier town, just as real Indian towns were changing around them.

Narayan lived most of his life in [[@mysuru|Mysuru]], and many readers see that city in Malgudi's streets. The town has a river, the Sarayu, and a [[@indian-railways|railway station]], which Narayan said was the first thing he pictured.

In 1986, the actor and director Shankar Nag turned Narayan's stories into a series for Doordarshan. At a time when most Indian homes had a single channel, millions of families watched it together.

Nag filmed most of it in Agumbe, a village in the rainforests of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], with red-tiled houses, narrow streets and almost constant rain. Local people acted alongside professional actors. Narayan's younger brother, R. K. Laxman, India's best-known cartoonist, drew the sketches that appear in the opening and between scenes. The music, with its famous humming, was composed by L. Vaidyanathan.

The young actor Master Manjunath played Swami and became one of the most recognisable child stars of Indian television.

Narayan's sentences are short and plain. He rarely explains his characters' feelings. He shows what they do and lets you work out the rest, often with a quiet joke at the end.

Because his stories avoid big events, they have aged slowly. A boy who hates maths homework, a shopkeeper worried about money, a child who wants a dog: these could be anywhere. That is why Malgudi has readers in the USA and Britain as well as India, and why some families now watch the old series on their phones, decades after it first aired.
